title: Elucidating the Role of DNA Shape in CRISPR Target Discrimination
text:
The proposed work will uncover intrinsic shape of DNA duplexes and elucidate its roles in CRSIPR Cas9
and Cas12a target discrimination. Information learned will be incorporated into algorithms for enhancing CRISPR
targeting specificity, ultimately advancing CRISPR-based technologies for effective genome manipulation in both
basic research and therapeutic development.

title: High-throughput cellular genetics to connect noncoding variants to coronary artery disease genes
text:
This study will provide important new insights into how genetic variants in humans influence risk for coronary
artery disease (responsible for a quarter of all deaths in the US), which could support the discovery and
development of much-needed new classes of therapies. It will also establish a novel, generalizable method that
could dramatically accelerate the discovery of biological mechanisms for many other common diseases.

title: Dissecting the Etiology of The Lewy Body Dementias
text:
We propose studies to determine whether dementia with Lewy bodies (DLB) and Parkinson disease with
dementia (PDD) are neuropathologically, molecularly and genetically distinct neurodegenerative diseases using
novel probes that distinguish different species of alpha-synuclein, a major component of Lewy bodies (LBs), and
new artificial intelligence (AI) approaches that may reveal distinct features of the two conditions in post-mortem
brains. We reported the first DLB genome-wide association study and will now use a similar approach to identify
genetic determinants that predict the neuropathology and/or clinical symptoms of PDD patients and develop
novel stratification schemes for DLB and PDD patients. We will use snRNA-seq and spatial transcriptomics on
brain tissue to determine if transcriptomic signatures can distinguish DLB and PDD patients and be used to
design new neuropathology labels and AI algorithms aimed at distinguishing DLB from PDD brains.

title: Research training in Pediatric Endocrinology
text:
Pediatric Endocrinology is one of the smallest pediatric subspecialties. Obesity and diabetes
(both type 1 and type 2) in youth are on the rise with major current and future impact on overall
health. Very few pediatric endocrinologists have had adequate training and mentorship in
research, and thus lack the skills to perform cutting-edge research in pediatric endocrine
diseases. This training grant will educate a new generation of pediatric endocrinologists and
Ph.D. scientists, who can play a role as leaders and researchers in pediatric endocrinology and
diabetes.

title: Molecular Mechanisms of Atrial Development and Regeneration
text:
We currently do not understand the mechanisms that underlie the majority of congenital heart defects, which are
the most common birth defects, or how to efficient repair injured hearts. This project will provide a greater
understanding of the causes of congenital heart defects, normal heart development and regeneration. Ultimately,
the information gleaned may allow the generation of novel therapies able to prevent congenital heart defects and
regenerate injured hearts in children and adults.

title: Tumor Biology and Microenvironment Program
text: The overarching goal of the Tumor Biology and Microenvironment (TBM) Program is to investigate tumor cell-autonomous (intrinsic) processes that underlie signaling pathways and cancer stemness and tumor cell-extrinsic mechanisms by which stromal niche factors and immune components modulate malignancy. Advancing the HICCC’s strategic focus on fostering impactful discovery science and accelerating translation to innovative clinical research, Members pursue studies of novel immunotherapies and other stromal-targeted therapeutics and incorporate new findings and innovative approaches (e.g., 3D organoid cultures) for translation to pre-clinical applications and development of early-stage clinical trials. Co-Leaders, Michael Shen, PhD, Barbara Pro, MD, and Timothy C Wang, MD, bring complementary expertise to the Program’s 64 Members who, in 2024, held $24M of cancerfocused peer-reviewed funding (+45% from the previous renewal), with $10M (42%) from NCI (more than doubled since the previous renewal), $11M (47%) from other NIH sources, and $2.6M (11%) from other peer-reviewed agencies. Members published 548 peer-reviewed cancer research papers over the project period, of which 17% were intra-programmatic, 32% inter-programmatic, and 82% inter-institutional. Notably, 45% were in journals with impact factors >10 and 23% (of total) >20. TBM Program Member-led clinical trials accrued 558 subjects to interventional trials, of which 18% were to investigator-initiated. The TBM Program pursues three interrelated Specific Aims: (1) Investigate stemness and plasticity through studies of cell intrinsic processes that drive tumor initiation and malignant progression to identify strategies to target these processes; (2) Analyze the stromal microenvironment to understand stromal-epithelial cell interactions and understand how stromal niche components modulate tumor growth; and (3) Investigate the tumor immune microenvironment to elucidate the interaction of immune cell with cancer cells and the mechanisms of resistance to immunotherapy. Working with the Community Outreach and Engagement Office, TBM Program research relevant for the catchment area includes in prostate, breast, liver, hematologic, and head-and-neck cancers. The TBM Program fosters interaction of Members (intra- and inter-programmatic) through meetings and retreats, development funds, support of multi-investigator grant proposals, Shared Resources, and strategic faculty recruitments. TBM Program Co-Leaders and Members also play key role in Cancer Research Training and Education Coordination, with mentorship of early-stage researchers through training grants, fellowships, and career development awards. Future goals of the Program include strategic recruitment of senior and junior faculty focused on the cancer stem cells and the tumor microenvironment, as well as increased focus on therapies that target tumor cells and the microenvironment (e.g., cell and gene therapy) and translation of discoveries to clinical trials.

title: Mechanism and Evolution of Circadian Clocks and Photoperiodism
text:
RELEVANCE TO PUBLIC HEALTH: This project will clarify the organization of circadian and photoperiodic
timing systems at levels that were heretofore unreachable. Biological clocks have been found to be crucial for
physical and mental health; cancer, metabolic disorders, cardiovascular disease, and depression are
associated with the disruption of these timing systems by genetic and/or environmental disturbance.
Understanding the how and why of chronobiology & its regulation along with the development of therapies to
properly phase sleep will allow us to enhance health, performance, and well-being of humans suffering from
many types of mental and/or metabolic disorders.

title: Technology and Data Science Core
text: The Clinical Research Center for the Improved Prevention, Diagnosis, and Treatment of Vocal Hyperfunction (VHCRC) brings together a multidisciplinary team of experienced and productive investigators to pursue a comprehensive program of research focused on the study of hyperfunctional voice disorders. The Technology and Data Science Core (Tech Core) is a critical component of the VHCRC and provides central services and resources related to include procurement, setup, and maintenance of technology and equipment at the Massachusetts General Hospital Voice Center (MGH Voice Center) and Boston Medical Center; data quality checks and pre-processing; signal/image processing resources and services for all Projects; centralized database management integrating data types from all Projects; statistical and machine learning services to all Projects; and data sharing with Project collaborators and the broader research community. The Tech Core is primarily housed at the MGH Voice Center and includes a state-of-the-art voice clinic, the Voice and Speech Laboratory for vocal function testing, and the Laryngeal Surgery Research Laboratories for technology development and ongoing device maintenance. The Tech Core will provide biostatistical consulting expertise to VHCRC investigators through a subaward to the MGH Institute of Health Professions, especially with respect to the analysis of longitudinal data, latent profile analysis (unsupervised clustering for subtyping), structural equation modeling, and hierarchical linear modeling. The Tech Core also has a subaward to the MIT Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence Laboratory to provide advanced machine learning services (supervised classification, unsupervised clustering, and deep learning) to VHCRC investigators. The VHCRC will be greater than the sum of its parts because the Tech Core will increase project effectiveness by centralizing labor-intensive database organizational tasks, retrieving and organizing data regarding standard clinical voice assessment and treatment services for enrolled patients, performing advanced voice analysis, and managing data quality through automatic and semi-automatic pre-processing of thousands of hours of ambulatory participant data. The Tech Core will effectively integrate data types obtained by all Projects into a centralized, multidimensional voice database that will be organized, catalogued, and available to VHCRC investigators and the broader research community. The Tech Core will coordinate the sharing of high-quality data in a timely manner and, in conjunction with the Administrative Core, facilitate regular communication among all research teams to stimulate ongoing research progress.

title: Central auditory processing of natural sound category following sensorineural hearing loss
text:
While modern hearing aids offer substantial benefits, individuals with sensorineural hearing loss still struggle to
understand complex sounds in noisy environments. Addressing these persistent challenges requires insight into
how the auditory cortex processes complex sounds in normal hearing, how hearing loss disrupts this processing,
and how these changes impact perception. Leveraging advanced neurophysiological, computational, and
behavioral methods, the proposed project will characterize cortical coding degradations and behavioral deficits
due to noise-induced hearing loss and develop audio-processing algorithms to mitigate these deficits.

title: Cis-aconitate decarboxylase (ACOD1) in PMN-MDSC and prostate cancer progression
text:
Most patients with advanced prostate cancer respond poorly to immune checkpoint therapy (ICT). Although
recent preclinical and clinical studies have shed some light into the mechanisms underlying the
immunoresistance in prostate cancer, the cellular and molecular basics underlying immunoresistance in prostate
cancer remain poorly characterized. The proposed work will determine whether cis-aconitate decarboxylase
(ACOD1) regulates the functions of polymorphonuclear myeloid-derived suppressor cells (PMN-MDSCs) to
promotes prostate cancer progression and resistance to ICT.

title: Functional and therapeutic roles of the Hedgehog signaling in meibomian glands development, renewal and dysfunction
text:
Meibomian gland dysfunction is considered the leading cause of dry eye disease, a multifactorial
debilitating disease of the ocular surface with a global prevalence ranging from 5 to 50%. This
study will elucidate the role of components of the Hedgehog pathway in Meibomian gland
development and renewal. It will also define the therapeutic advantage in targeting the Hedgehog
signaling cascade using hydrogel-mediated drug delivery systems to counteracting Meibomian
gland dysfunction.

title: Investigating the mechanisms of reduced neuron generation in Down Syndrome
text:
RESEARCH NARRATIVE
Individuals with Down syndrome (DS, T21) have reduced cortical volume, fewer neurons and smaller
progenitor pools but how the extra copy of human chromosome 21 (HSA21) causes these features
remains unanswered. Proper expansion of neural progenitor cells (NPCs) is crucial to generating the
appropriate number of neurons, so I hypothesize that increased NPC death, prolonged cell cycle length,
and/or early cell cycle exit contribute to reduced progenitor pools in T21. The project in this fellowship
will test the contribution of these three non-exclusive mechanisms to reduced progenitor pools in T21
and identify upstream molecular and cellular pathways to provide mechanistic insight into the impact of
T21 on neurogenesis.

title: Improving Suicide Risk Prediction in Racial, Ethnic, and Linguistic Minority Youth
text: The proportion of pediatric emergency department or inpatient visits due to suicidal thoughts and behaviors (STB) has doubled in recent years. Machine learning (ML) and natural language processing (NLP) with electronic health records (EHR) have advanced suicide risk identification, with potential to fill the need for sustainable and scalable practice-based resources with near-term impact. Despite the near-term promise of ML and NLP with EHR data for advancing suicide risk prediction, several important issues need to be addressed before ML-derived tools can be broadly and optimally implemented in practice-based settings. Of particular concern is that such ML algorithms may perform unevenly across racial, ethnic, and linguistic minority youth, specifically Black, Hispanic, and youth whose language of care is not English. Trends in suicide attempts over the past decade have remained higher or increased among Black and Hispanic youth compared to White peers; there are few data on youth whose language of care is not English. These demographic groups have been less likely to have their healthcare data included in the development of these ML algorithms. Within this context, algorithms trained on EHR data linked to individual and area-level risk factors and suicide assessment measures (Columbia Suicide Severity Rating Scale; C-SSRS) has potential to improve suicide risk prediction. Individual social risk factors include self-reported access to food, housing, utilities, healthcare, and safe relationships. Area-level factors include rates of residential segregation and stability, crime, civic engagement; access to healthcare; and economic measures, such as rates of poverty, food insecurity, and unemployment. The portability (and thus scalability) of ML algorithms across settings needs also to be demonstrated. Our current objective is therefore to develop EHR-derived ML suicide risk algorithms that (i) minimize inaccuracy against groups treated in community health settings; (ii) are portable across settings; and (iii) incorporate low-burden indices of general and population-relevant suicide risk. We will develop ML algorithms with EHR data for prospective prediction of suicide risk for youth within 3 months of inpatient discharge across 2 psychiatric inpatient services; determine the portability of these algorithms across the 2 sites; and evaluate the added predictive value of individual- and area-level variables and C-SSRS data collected as part of standard care. Our first aim is to develop prediction algorithms using EHR data to classify risk for STBs within 3 months of discharge. We will evaluate the relative performance of co-trained versus locally trained ML algorithms from two busy pediatric psychiatric inpatient sites to assess their portability. Our second aim is to evaluate the incremental value of individual and area-level variables and C-SSRS data in classifying suicide risk in youth. As an exploratory aim, we will evaluate the performance of the algorithms developed in Aims 1 and 2 for specific subsamples. The current project directly addresses NIMH/National Action Alliance for Suicide Prevention’s Aspirational Goal to improve evaluation of suicide risk among a variety of populations and settings through feasible and scalable assessment strategies. It does so by focusing on youth across a range of backgrounds at risk for worse health outcomes.

title: Role of norovirus capsid dynamics in adaptive immune evasion
text:
Noroviruses are responsible for almost a fifth of all cases of gastroenteritis worldwide and are responsible for
~200 million cases worldwide among children less than 5 years old, leading to ~50,000 deaths every year. We
recently demonstrated that mouse norovirus reversibly switches between a structure recognized by antibodies
to one activated for receptor binding in the gut that we hypothesize evolved to aggressively avoid host adaptive
immunity. This proposal will test this model using structural biology and in-vivo testing that could answer the
paradox of why immunity to norovirus is transient and will directly impact the development of vaccines and
therapeutics.

title: Unlocking the biomedical potential of microbial symbionts from complex ecosystems
text:
New therapeutics are desperately needed for the treatment of diseases with unmet needs, such
as infectious and immunological diseases. This proposal uses an ecology-driven approach to
discover new drugs from the microbiome of marine egg masses, which have ecological pressures
that are predicted to have driven the evolution of novel antibiotics and immunomodulating agents.
Chemical investigations into egg mass symbionts will lead to the discovery of novel chemistry and
has the potential to repopulate the drug pipeline.

title: Novel Ion Chemistry and Instrument Development for the Characterization of Proteins, Nucleic Acids, and Heterogeneous Bio-complexes via Tandem Mass Spectrometry
text:
This project is devoted to novel ion chemistries and instrumentation for mass measurement and
structural characterization of intact bio-polymers and their complexes. Emphasis is placed on the gas-
phase attachment of multiply-charged ions of selected mass and charge to oppositely-charged ions
derived from complex bio-polymer mixtures, including heterogeneous complexes, such as molecular
machines and viruses. This effort addresses key limitations in the current state-of-the-art in top-down
proteomics and native mass spectrometry.

title: A Multiplex Protein Biomarker-Based Immunoassay for the Early Detection of Bladder Cancer and its Implications in Tumor Biology
text:
The project seeks to demonstrate feasible in the conduct of an early detection study in individuals at high risk
of developing bladder cancer and to evaluate a relevant rodent model, capable of identifying novel biomarkers,
which can be applied in the clinic.

title: Molecular subtyping of dry eye disease: A machine learning approach using tear fluid proteins
text:
Dry eye disease (DED) is one of the most common reasons people seek eye care, with symptoms including
dryness, burning, a gritty sensation, chronic eye pain, discomfort, irritation, and variable vision. Diagnosing and
treating DED is challenging due to its diverse causes, including reduced tear production, abnormalities in the
tear lipid layer, and associations with systemic diseases such as rheumatoid arthritis and Sjögren’s disease.
This project will utilize tear fluid biomarkers and machine learning algorithms to identify distinct DED subgroups
based on their molecular mechanisms, enabling more precise diagnostics and personalized treatments tailored
to the underlying drivers of the disease.

title: Presenilin and APP in the Brain
text:
Title: Presenilin and APP in the Brain
Narrative: Mutations in the PSEN and APP genes are linked to familial Alzheimer's disease (FAD), and PS is
the catalytic subunit of g-secretase, which cleaves APP to release Ab. In this competing renewal application, we
propose to examine whether APP mutations impair g-secretase and compromise neuronal survival and to
genetically investigate glial contributions to AD pathogenesis. The completion of the proposed studies will bridge
the gap in the FAD pathogenic mechanism and will open new directions in AD therapeutic development.

title: Apply novel pathogenomic approaches to identify interpretable image QTLs for multiple normal tissues
text:
In this project, we will apply advanced statistical and AI methods to identify human genetic
variants that are associated with cellular and tissue morphology. The results can serve as
baselines for disease pathology research. This work will also enhance our understanding about
how genomic information determines tissue development and differentiation.
